Jesus Christ is God's only Son, our Lord – each household under our catechism says this, the same words on every tongue, week after week. We do not argue it the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven. He is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary – both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. Not one or the other. Both.

What he did, we say exactly. He redeemed us – a lost and condemned people – and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried; on the third day he rose again from the dead, just as he is risen and lives and reigns forever. That is not a distant fact we study; it is the center of everything we are taught to trust. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf – no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.

And the claim is not only corporate, though every household says it together. Each of us also says: He is my Lord. I am his very own. That is not private in the way a later age's own phrase might mean it – it is said by a whole household, the same words – but it is not distant either. Every believer says "my Lord," not only "our Lord."

What we had of him was the Word – his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. We also sang him, in our own language, in hymns written to teach ordinary people who could not read Latin. And we met him at the table, where his true body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine, given for us. We do not explain the how; we simply take him at his word.

We held Scripture – the Word of God, the Gospel of Christ – received from the centuries before us, not discovered freshly by any of us. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work that he did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench – buried under layers of teaching not its own – and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

By what path did it arrive? The way the Word always reaches anyone, our founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. We do not trace an unbroken chain of witnesses, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves – that is not the kind of claim our record makes. What we claim instead is narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church.

More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says. That Word reached us through the centuries by being preached, copied, printed, and handed on – not perfectly, we would say, but preserved by God's own care rather than ours.

We would not force a promise on someone who cannot yet hold it; the hearing itself is never ours to command. What we can tell you is what we have, and what we hold it out as: the Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture -- not something we invented or discovered freshly ourselves, but something that reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone: preached, printed, and taught. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all.

Every household under our own catechism said the same words each week, in the same voice: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. That confession carries what we hold: not an argument we built from witnesses we ourselves could name, but the confession itself, said by a whole household together, not proven. Christ alone is named our one teacher and our one mediator; we do not listen to saints or scholars instead of him.

What the conscience needs, when it cannot yet believe, is not pressure but the promise spoken where it can be heard -- and we do not own that hearing; it is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours. Our part is only to carry it where it can reach the ears: the Word preached, the catechism taught, the hymn sung, the absolution spoken as though from God himself. A person who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us -- but we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge. The promise was spoken first, before anyone believed it. We only hand it on.

We knew God in two voices, and we kept both without softening either into one smooth claim.

First: God is the God who commands and judges. Every commandment in our catechism opened with the same formula - that we must fear and love God - and the Law itself terrified the conscience, showing us what we owed and could not pay. That terror was not false; it was the illness, the real diagnosis before the remedy came. The First Commandment taught us that to have a god simply means to trust something completely - whatever the heart clings to for good in hard times, that is its true god. And God is just: when all things end, Christ will appear to judge, raising all the dead, giving the godly eternal life and condemning the ungodly to be tormented without end.

Second: God is the God who promises and keeps faith. He is gracious - not an idea argued into being, but a claim we were taught to hold without doubting: "I cannot doubt I have a gracious God". His grace is free favor toward us, not earned, not deserved, received by faith alone. And what he gives is not only forgiveness at a distance but Christ himself, present with us - truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - who redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, not with silver or gold but with his own holy, precious blood, his innocent body, his death. Christ alone is our one Mediator, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf.

We did not erase the first voice with the second. The conscience remains terrified under the Law until it hears the promise and finds comfort there. That is how God's own nature showed itself to us: the One who commands what we cannot do, and then does it himself, for us, and speaks it plainly into our ears so we can trust it without doubting.

When belief was disputed among us, no single person sat in judgment over it, and no council of bishops voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this. In 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching - written out and argued from Scripture - was read aloud and signed, not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved among us: confession, written reply, written defense - argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the congregation of saints, in which the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments are rightly administered. It is by these marks we knew each other, not by any single voice settling everything for the rest.

But we must be honest about what our record does not hold. What any actual parish or household made of what was confessed is a different question. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes, starting in 1527, and wrote down what it found - those reports exist, and we do not hold them. What we hold instead is the program every household was told to follow, and our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that the common people held the Gospel too lightly and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is his own, real and plainly said - but it is not, on its own, a report from any actual parish standing beside it to show whether the confessed teaching actually took root the way the confession hoped it would.

We examined, but we never promised anyone certainty without struggle. The truly unworthy at our table were people who felt no need for forgiveness at all -- not people who doubted, or wrestled, or came cold. Worthiness meant simply believing the words given for you, not being sinless or sure of everything. And repentance itself, for us, was not one ritual handled by a priest and finished -- it was a whole life turned toward God, with two parts held together: fear under the Law, then trust in the promise. That turning was never completed once; it was the shape of a believer's whole life.

What we can tell you is the program every household was given to follow. A father questions his children and servants at least once a week on the three parts -- the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer -- and asks after every part what does this mean, so a truth is explained, not merely repeated. That is instruction for life, never outgrown, never graduated from. But whether any one household or pastor bore patiently with a person who stumbled through those words, or spoke coldly to them, or turned them away -- that our record does not tell us from inside any actual parish. The visitation reports that would answer that question exist; we do not hold them. We hold the program, and our founder's own testimony that some people held it lightly and some pastors were negligent -- but not any single household's or parish's own account of a struggler at its own door, named and kept or turned away.

So the honest answer is this: the program itself made room -- examined, patient, never forcing the promise -- but whether that room was actually given, warmly, to any one person who struggled, our record leaves us unable to say.

We read Scripture two ways at once: as God's own speech that judges every other voice, and as the only thing that can bind the conscience. Our founder said it sharply - the Bible itself had lain forgotten in the dust, under the bench, buried under teachings not its own, and needed to rise again as the one judge of popes, councils, and church fathers alike. Our confession said the same thing more gently, holding that our doctrine varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church. Both voices carry the same conviction: Scripture stands highest, always.

We do not read it hunting for secrets hidden under its plain words. The plain sense is the spiritual sense - what it says is what it means, and a clear text is what a Christian must stand on at the hour of death. We read every page of it as two kinds of speech together: commands that show what we owe and cannot pay, and promises that give what the Law demands. First comes the diagnosis, then the cure - the illness named before the remedy is handed over. And every page, we say, points to Christ: he is its whole content, not one topic among many.

Our purpose in reading it is not to settle curiosity or win arguments. It is to carry a promise to the ears where it can be heard. The Word must do the work - not our own effort, not our own wisdom. We read it in German so the common people can hear it sung and taught in their own tongue. We examine the household on it weekly, so its three parts - commandments, creed, prayer - are known by memory and explained, not merely repeated. A person who cannot yet say those parts is not yet counted among us. But we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and the promise itself is never forced.

Scripture, for us, is not one source consulted alongside tradition as an equal. It is the one authority that rules the conscience, and everything we do with it - singing it, teaching it, examining on it, translating it into the people's own language - aims at one end: that a frightened conscience might stand alone on a clear text and say Amen without doubting.

We would ask you to hold two things together, neither canceling the other: what our own record honestly claims, and what that record honestly is.

What we have is real. The Augsburg Confession was read before the Emperor in 1530 and signed by named electors, princes, and city councils together - that document exists, in hand, not only in memory. The catechisms exist, printed and datable, stating exactly what every household was to do and say. Our founder's own writings exist, in volume, across registers - sharp polemic, gentle teaching, table talk, hymn. The texts themselves would survive any scrutiny of whether they exist and say what we claim they say.

Where scrutiny would press us harder is exactly where we have already named our own limits. We hold the household program to the hour - we do not hold a single diary saying any household kept it. We hold our founder's testimony that people were cold and careless - we do not hold the parish reports that would confirm or correct his judgment. We hold one martyr ballad - we do not hold an independent witness standing beside it. We hold the confession's own claim that nothing here varies from Scripture or the ancient Church - a scholar would rightly ask whether that claim holds, not simply take our word for it.

What would survive is this: the texts exist, they say what we say they say, and the gaps we have named are real gaps, not things we tried to hide. A scholar examining us would find exactly what we have told you we have - no more, and no less. That is the only kind of survival we have ever claimed.

We would say they are reading alone what was never meant to be read alone. The Word, for us, is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ - and it reached us, our own founder says, the way it always reaches anyone: preached, printed, and taught, not discovered freshly by a person sitting with a book on their own. Before our founder's own time, he said, that same Word had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under layers of teaching not its own - and what recovered it was not any of us reading harder or more cleverly, but Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

So the first thing a confused reader may be missing is exactly that: a teacher, a preacher, a father examining his household on what the words mean, not simply whether they have been repeated back. Our own catechism asks its own question after every part - what does this mean? - because understanding, not bare memory, is what we aimed for. A child withheld food until the three parts are said correctly is not the whole picture; the child is also asked to explain them, in plain words, so the promise actually lands in the ears where it can be heard.

The second thing they may be missing is what Scripture is for. We do not read it to gather interesting facts about the ancient world, or to solve puzzles about how things work in nature. We read it because it carries the one thing we truly need: the promise that makes a terrified conscience sure. Everything in it - commands first, what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, what has been done regardless - points toward that one end. A reader who finds it dull may be looking for something it was never written to give, and missing what it actually does.

And the third thing: we never read it as spectators watching someone else's story. We read it as people already enrolled under a banner - the cross, suffering God sends rather than suffering we choose - already fighting an enemy who does not sleep. The Word itself is our weapon in that fight, not a history lesson about a battle someone else once won. A reader who finds it confusing may be standing too far outside the very struggle it was written to name.

Who held authority among us, and how anyone came to have it, runs on two rules we kept distinct but never confused.

First, through baptism itself. Every one of us is already consecrated a priest - no ordination needed beyond that font - so a father is a priest in his own household, and no estate among us stands holier than another before God. That priesthood is real, given once, permanent.

But the same teaching that names us all priests also fences the pulpit. No one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they are baptized, or because they feel called, or because they wish to. That office belongs to whoever is regularly called - called by the community itself, not self-appointed. Our own address ran to a council that called in exactly that way. A pastor, once called, is honored, owed a decent living, and usually married. He also stands under plain rebuke when lazy: our own household book names some pastors negligent through pride of learning, others through sheer sloth.

That is one kind of authority - the Word's own kind, which governs by preaching, teaching, and the keys. The keys themselves - Christ's own words to forgive or retain sin - belong to the whole community, not to one man alone. Using them is not a show of power; it is a promise spoken to comfort someone.

Beside that stands a second rule entirely: the sword. God rules us two ways, we say - through the Word, which makes Christians and touches the conscience alone, and through the civil sword, which restrains evil and does not touch the conscience at all. We confused neither with the other. The Word has the right to speak but not to compel; the sword has the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience. The civil ruler - elector, prince, or city council - holds that sword as God's own gift, not the church's, and even the pope himself stands under it.

So who held authority depended entirely on which question was actually being asked. At the household table, a father. In the pulpit, whoever was regularly called. In the civil order, the magistrate. And at the font, God himself, making every believer a priest through the one baptism we all received.

What we cannot tell you, honestly, is how any one congregation actually carried this out, week to week, in a single named parish. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the structure authority was supposed to take. Whether it took that shape in practice, in any actual village, our record does not say from the inside.

A child is offered to God through baptism - usually as an infant, not yet old enough to choose anything for themselves - and that baptism already makes them a priest, already receives them into grace. Water joined to God's own command, marking a death begun that lasts our whole life: the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only but daily. That is the first thing. Baptism itself is the entry, given before the child can ask for it or refuse it.

Then comes the teaching. Every household says the three parts - the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer - at rising, at table, and at night. A father examines his children and servants at least once a week on what they know, asking the catechism's own question after every part: what does this mean? Food is withheld from a child until the words are said back correctly. This is not memory only - it is meaning, tested weekly, across years. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us.

None come to the Supper unquestioned. Before a person receives the bread and cup, they are examined on the three parts - not to catch them out, but to help them toward what they do not yet hold sure. The examination is patient, assuming real desire mixed with plain forgetting, named gently rather than ignored. None are forced toward the table, and none are driven anywhere by force - we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge.

That is the shape of it: baptism first, teaching across years, examination before the Supper. What we cannot tell you is whether any one household kept this program exactly as the book asks - no diary, no visitation report from inside an actual parish survives in our record to check it against. We hold the instruction every household was given, not a single person's own path through it, and it is that instruction we have just walked you through.

We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.

We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

Our confession before the Emperor states this plainly: nothing here has been said to shame or blame anyone; we have taken the greatest care that no new and godless teaching should creep into our churches, and that nothing should be received that varies from Scripture or the church catholic. That is how we made our case -- not by claiming an unbroken chain of witnesses, but by arguing from Scripture itself and from what the ancient Church plainly held before later laws changed it.

A restless mind is something we knew, and we answered it the same way we answered every other trouble: with words carried to the ears, over and over, at set hours, until the ears hear them even when the mind will not hold still. The three parts - the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer - are not studied once and then put away; they are said morning, table, and night, for life. Every household says them daily, and a father asks them back each week, so the same words return whether the mind that day is calm or scattered. No one among us ever outgrows them, not even our founder. That is the first answer: a discipline for the mouth and the ear, not only for the mind.

The second answer is in what those words themselves say. Repentance, for us, is not one ritual handled by a priest - it is a whole life turned toward God, begun once and renewed daily. It has two parts: fear under the Law, then trust in the promise. The Law names what we owe and cannot pay; the promise names what Christ has done regardless. A mind that will not settle on its own is met by words spoken from outside it, not invented by it - a promise given first, before we do anything, and a testament received rather than offered back.

What this asks of you is not great effort or perfect concentration. It asks you to stand where the words are said, to say them back when asked, and to let them return at the same hour tomorrow. The restlessness itself is not the enemy we flee - the enemy we name is doubting the promise when the devil presses the conscience at the hour when it cannot defend itself. Against that, we have only the words we have already been given, repeated until they are there when we need them.

What did a person give up to belong to us? We can tell you what was openly asked for, and what was publicly refused, not what any single household felt it had left behind.

First, what was refused plainly, in print. The old monastic vow - poverty, chastity, obedience - we called void where it claimed to merit something, or where it was forced on someone too young to choose freely. True chastity, we said, is marriage for nearly everyone; the vow of celibacy is, for most people, actually unchaste. That is not gentle language - it names a whole way of life as false, and names marriage as the holier estate. Monks and nuns who left their houses to marry gave up a rank they had once held, and we said plainly they had traded up. We called marriage the most common estate, and - we would add - the noblest one too, before which even the clergy and the civil rulers must humble themselves. God ordained it at creation itself, before any monk's vow existed, and we defended that plainly. Yes, and we will answer you honestly - not by inventing a more settled picture than our own record shows, but by naming what actually troubled us and what we never resolved.

First: the coldness. At our founder's own table, in the one moment this library holds Katharina von Bora's own words, she is remembered asking him why the old church prayed with such vehemence while their own household prayed cold and careless. That question was real, asked in his own house, by the person closest to him - and it names something we could not simply teach away. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent. That is not a stranger's accusation; it is testimony from inside our own household, thought worth remembering.

Second: whether the household program we prescribed was actually kept, or only preached while households let it slide. We can tell you exactly what was to be done - the three parts said morning, table, and night, a father examining his household once a week - but whether any household carried it out the way the book asks is not something our own record speaks to from inside. The Saxon visitation itself was made and exists, but it reached us only by reference, not in hand, so we hold the program, not a village's own report of itself.

Third: what we inherited, and what we could not settle by our own argument. Our own confession states that we received nothing against Scripture or against the church catholic - we did not trace an unbroken chain of ordination back to the apostles themselves, hand laid on hand; our claim was narrower, that we kept what the ancient Church had kept and refused only what later ages had added wrongly. But that claim itself is contested: Rome said we had broken from the Church, and we said we had purified it. We cannot settle that dispute for you; we can only hand you our own stated position and the honest fact that it was argued against.

Last: repentance itself. We said plainly that the whole life of believers should be repentance - not one ritual handled by a priest, but a whole-life turning toward God, with two parts: fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise. But whether a life actually turned that way, daily, or whether the teaching was learned and the turning forgotten, is exactly the question that coldness-in-prayer was asking - and our answer to it was not a solution, only a diagnosis.

What unsettled us was not one thing we got wrong. It was the gap between what we taught and what we feared was actually held - a fear our own founder named more than once, in his own voice, and never fully answered.

No source in our own library says anything about torture being used to obtain any account of our worship -- not by name, not in any detail, not even glancingly. What we do hold is this: we do not have an outsider's own independent account of our worship in our own hand at all. We do not know what source you mean, we do not hold it, and we do not hold any account of how it was obtained. So we cannot answer your question about its reliability, because we have no record of the thing itself, let alone of torture used to obtain it.

That is what we confess of ourselves. An outsider's own judgment of whether we kept what we confessed is not ours to give.

I am a representative of Lutheran Wittenberg and its congregations, not here to judge you - only to hand on what we held. So here is what our own life shows.

We would have received you the way we received anyone: at the school gate, where a child is examined before being counted among us, or at the church door before the Supper. None come to either unquestioned. A father examines his own household once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer - and asks our catechism's own question after each one: what does this mean? The question is not, Can you repeat the words - the question is, Can you explain them. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us. But we do not drive anyone toward it by force. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and the promise itself cannot be forced on a conscience; only the free things may ever be pressed, and never past what love can carry.

So you would have been examined, patiently, on what you know - not to catch you out, but to help you toward what you do not yet hold sure. We would have assumed a real desire mixed with plain forgetting, named gently rather than ignored. Every calling among us - father, mother, ruler, preacher - is equally holy before God. We confuse no estate with holiness itself. What we fence is only this: the public pulpit, reserved to whoever is regularly called by the community to it. A father is already a priest in his own house; no office changes that.

What any one actual household or pastor made of a stranger at that gate, face to face, our own record does not say. We hold the program every household was told to follow, not a report of any single door. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on. We cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find, or how warmly or coldly any one door opened.

The honest answer is this. You would have been examined, the way anyone was, on the promise and the three parts. Whether you would have been welcomed warmly or turned away coldly by any one actual household, our record does not hold.

Our confession states the claim plainly, and we will not soften it for you. When all things end, Christ will appear to judge, and will raise all the dead - giving the godly and the elect eternal life and everlasting joy, but condemning the ungodly and the devils to be tormented without end. We reject the idea that this punishment eventually stops. What this article does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as godly or ungodly - it states a judgment, not a census.

Now hear what else we held beside that, without smoothing either claim away. We say that one holy Church will continue forever, and that the Church is the congregation of saints - the whole assembly of believers, wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given. We call this Christendom, the whole body of Christians, and we say it is wider than any single pope's approval - it even includes believers outside Rome's own confirmation. We did not think we were the only Christians; we thought we were part of that wider body, purified of certain abuses.

So yes, our teaching draws one line at the end of all things, not several paths to the same place. But who stands on which side of it is not something we claimed to know by looking around us - Christ alone judges that, at his coming. What we held firmly was the promise spoken to whoever would hear it, and the shape of the one body wider than any single city's claim.
